title: Did climate change make Australia’s Black Summer fires more likely?
text:
In the summer of 2019/20, bushfires burned more than 19 million hectares of Australia, killed 34 people directly and destroyed nearly 5,900 buildings. Afterwards, a lot of people asked the same question: was this just a terrible run of weather, or did climate change play a part?
It matters because the answer changes what we should expect next. If it was bad luck, another season like it is rare. If climate change made it more likely, seasons like it will keep getting more common.
This post explains what one group of researchers found (Oldenborgh et al. 2021).

The short version: climate change made the extreme heat and fire weather behind Black Summer clearly more likely. It did not make the drought more likely.

title: Did climate change make Australia’s Black Summer fires more likely?
text:
In the summer of 2019/20, bushfires burned more than 19 million hectares of Australia, killed 34 people directly and destroyed nearly 5,900 buildings. Afterwards, a lot of people asked the same question: was this just a terrible run of weather, or did climate change play a part?
It matters because the answer changes what we should expect next. If it was bad luck, another season like it is rare. If climate change made it more likely, seasons like it will keep getting more common.
This post explains what one group of researchers found (Oldenborgh et al. 2021).

title: Did climate change make Australia’s Black Summer fires more likely?
text:
Analysis: what the evidence shows
Where the evidence comes from. The researchers did not run a new experiment. They used 40 years of detailed weather records, temperature and rainfall measurements going back to 1900, and 11 sets of climate model simulations. They asked how likely a season this extreme is today, compared with a world without human-caused warming.
What they found. Think of loaded dice. Climate change doesn’t roll the dice for a particular fire, but it makes the bad rolls come up more often. Table 1 sets out the results for each ingredient of a bad fire season.



Table 1: What climate change did to the odds of each fire ingredient










What was measured
How much more likely than in the early 1900s
How sure are they?




Extreme heat
At least 2 times
Very sure


Fire weather index (heat, dryness and wind combined)
At least 1.3 times in the models, 4 times or more in the observations
Sure, and probably an underestimate


Monthly severity rating
About 2 times in the models, 9 times or more in the observations
Same direction, less certain


Drought
No clear change
Not linked to climate change






Figure 1 shows the same results as a chart. Heat stands out, and drought is the one measure that sits on the “no change” line.








Figure 1: Heat is the clearest signal. Drought shows no change. Bars show the minimum increase in likelihood, from the model results in Oldenborgh et al. (2021).





What this tells us about the problem. Back to the question: was Black Summer just bad luck? Not entirely. The heat and fire weather part of it was made more likely by human-caused warming. The drought part was mostly down to natural patterns in the Indian and Pacific oceans, so the dry conditions were not a climate change effect.
What this doesn’t tell us. These numbers are minimums. The climate models tend to underestimate how much extreme heat has increased, so the real change is probably larger. The study also covers weather, not damage. How much a fire destroys depends on other things too, like where we build and how well we prepare.

title: Did climate change make Australia’s Black Summer fires more likely?
section: Conclusion: what it means for you
text:
Conclusion: what it means for you
The question was whether Black Summer was just bad luck. The research says no. Hotter, drier-feeling conditions that lead to dangerous fire weather are now at least twice as likely to occur as they were in the early 1900s, and the drought was the only ingredient that wasn’t linked to climate change.
For readers, the practical takeaway is that fire seasons like 2019/20 should be treated as a real and growing risk, not a one-off. That is worth knowing if you live in a fire-prone area, or if you are making decisions about where to buy, build or insure. The researchers’ own results are the best place to read more (Oldenborgh et al. 2021).

title: About
text:
Hi, I am Shravani. I’m a Master’s student at Monash University, based in Melbourne.
Before returning to study, I worked across banking, marketing and tech. That mix is why I enjoy turning data into something people can act on, which is what this blog is about.
This site is part of my ETC5523 Communicating with Data coursework. The main post turns a research paper on climate change and Australian bushfire risk into a plain-English summary.
